transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-05 14:00 PST / Duration ~48m
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Samira Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood Infra), Jane Park (NexaHealth ML Platform), Tom Liu (NexaHealth Lead ML Eng), Priya Singh (NexaHealth SecOps), Chris (Data Director)

Summary: Quick technical deep-dive on a recent accuracy regression after moving to an AWQ/GPTQ hybrid for cost reasons. Focus on: layerwise regression detection, precision gating (fallbacks per-layer), KV cache and batching interaction, and on-prem/VPC benchmarking plan.

00:00:00 Alex: ok hey everyone thanks for joining, can you see my screen?
00:00:05 Jane: yup, we can. thanks for setting this up. quick note, Priya's on from SecOps to ask a couple of compliance Qs.
00:00:12 Alex: great. quick round — i'll be brief, samira and diego from product infra. tue at a high level, what's the problem you're seeing?
00:00:22 Tom: yeah thanks. so we rolled a mixed quant strategy last week — we used g p t q for most of the trunk and AWQ for the attention layers to save about 3x on tokens. for most prompts latency and cost were fine, but we saw a measurable drop in our medical-qa accuracy on about 7% of prompts. it's subtle but important.
00:00:45 Samira: 7% is non-trivial. do you have examples of the failures? are they concentrated by prompt length or on certain output types?
00:00:51 Tom: mostly mid-length prompts, 40-160 tokens. the errors often look like hallucination or missing entities, sometimes the model truncates an answer. we'll upload the golden outputs.
00:01:03 Chris: and just to add, our SLA for retrieval accuracy is pretty strict for those intents. not acceptable in prod.
00:01:08 Diego: ok, couple quick clarifying Qs — are you on-prem or using our dedicated environment?
00:01:14 Jane: we're running on a VPC-connected on-prem cluster for data residency. the model is our fork of open-llm-large, patched to use the Redwood runtime.
00:01:23 Samira: good. that helps. i want to outline our approach: 1) reproduce locally with your prompt corpus 2) run layerwise quant bisect (int8/gptq/awq mixes) 3) inspect kv cache and batching interplay 4) propose per-layer precision gating or fallback rules and a rollout plan. sound ok?
00:01:42 Priya: i have a quick secops interjection: any changes to model binaries require our audit and keys. do you support KMS/HSM signing checks in the private package?
00:01:52 Diego: yes, our private runtime supports KMS-signed model artifacts and a hash verification flow. we'll share the runbook.
00:01:59 Tom: thanks. so during the regression the traces show increased attention norm variance, does that ring a bell?
00:02:07 Samira: yes, that can happen if certain layers quantize poorly — attention scales are sensitive. AWQ sometimes shifts scaling factors in softmax inputs and GPTQ layer-wise rounding can amplify it.
00:02:23 Alex: can you walk through what you mean by precision gating?
00:02:26 Samira: sure — instead of a global precision for the whole model, we make per-layer decisions. if layer N drops below a quality threshold in a probe we keep it at fp16 or fp8, otherwise quantize to int8. we also support dynamic fallbacks at runtime: if a request fails a confidence heuristic we re-run the request on a higher precision variant.
00:02:47 Tom: re-run? won't that double latency occasionally?
00:02:50 Samira: yes — that's the tradeoff. we try to confine re-runs to only problematic inputs using a cheap confidence check (e.g., logit gap, token entropy). for bulk workloads we prefer pre-deployment layer fixes via gating.
00:03:05 Jane: can gating be applied automatically based on a small eval set?
00:03:08 Samira: yea. our Optimize tool can suggest a layer list after running a 500-sample eval and recommends a candidate precision profile.
00:03:16 Chris: what's the overhead on KV cache when we enable fallback re-runs? any cache invalidation concerns?
00:03:20 Diego: good call. re-runs bypassing cache can increase per-token compute, but we can do hybrid: store KV cache for quantized runs too, with a cache-key that tags precision profile. so if a re-run uses a higher precision but same prefix, we won't hit the lower-precision cache. it is more cache space but prevents repeated compute on same prefixes.
00:03:40 Priya: how about security — storing multiple cache copies acceptable, compliance-wise?
00:03:44 Tom: from our side, extra cached artifacts must be encrypted-at-rest and rotate keys with KMS.
00:03:49 Diego: agreed — our KV cache layers support envelope encryption with customer KMS keys in VPC mode.
00:03:55 Alex: ok back to regression — Samira, what's your proposed bisect?
00:03:58 Samira: we'll run a layerwise delta test. step 1: take your quantized runtime and swap each layer to fp16 one-by-one while running the golden prompt set, measuring accuracy delta and latency. step 2: for any layer with big delta, test alternatives: fp8 with narrow mantissa, int8 with per-channel scaling, g p t q with different group sizes, and awq variants. step 3: evaluate combined configs and generate a precision gating policy.
00:04:27 Tom: how long does that take?
00:04:29 Samira: for a 70-layer model with 2k prompts, maybe 3-6 hours if we parallelize across 4 nodes. we'll need the prompt corpus and a small compute window.
00:04:38 Jane: we can carve a 4-hour window next week. hope that's enough.
00:04:42 Alex: good. any thoughts on kernel selection and latency jitter during these tests?
00:04:46 Diego: kernel selection matters a lot. on our runtime we pick kernels per-layer at load time based on model dims and target sequence lengths. but when you mix precisions, some kernels fall back to slower code paths. part of the bisect is capturing kernel choice and when we see slow fallbacks.
00:05:03 Tom: i remember seeing 'vectorized fallback' messages in logs — what's the recommended mitigation?
00:05:08 Diego: two options: change the quantization config to better match available kernels (e.g., align group sizes), or enable a different kernel set— we have an alternate fp8-optimized path that helps. but you may pay memory overhead.
00:05:20 Priya: from a security/process view, we need to know any change that requires recertification. is switching kernel path a big change?
00:05:27 Alex: operationally, we'd treat kernel-path changes as minor if we don't touch the model artifact; if the artifact changes we follow your policy. we'll document everything for audits.
00:05:36 Samira: another interesting data point — certain prompts with long retrieval prefixes interacted badly: the KV cache prefix length changes effective token distribution and produced edge-case attention saturations. that suggests the problem is both quantization and prefix distribution.
00:05:53 Tom: yes — many of our medical prompts have long context windows (retrieved notes) so KV caching behavior matters.
00:05:58 Alex: can we instrument prefix-length buckets in the bisect runs?
00:06:01 Samira: yes, we'll bucket by prefix lengths (0-64,65-256,>256) and report per-bucket accuracy.
00:06:08 Jane: perfect. also we need to know how batching affects the failure modes — we run high batching at night.
00:06:14 Diego: batching can smooth out quant noise for some kernels but exacerbate it for others because reduced per-request cache hits change activation distributions. we'll test multiple batching profiles (sync vs async, batch sizes 1,4,8,16).
00:06:29 Tom: i had a small note about warm KV cache vs cold starts — failures seemed more common on cold caches.
00:06:34 Samira: yep that maps to our experience; cold cache means more variance in early layers. fallback rules can be more aggressive for cold-start requests (e.g., prefer higher precision if cache-miss rate > X).
00:06:45 Chris: how do you suggest we roll out changes? small canary? ab-test?
00:06:49 Alex: standard pattern — canary with 1% traffic, run for X hours, monitor quality signals (our eval set) and latency SLOs; if stable, scale canary. we also support automatic rollback if quality dips.
00:06:59 Tom: will Redwood's console expose the per-route token cost delta when we change precision?
00:07:03 Diego: yes, the console shows per-token CPU/GPU time and estimated cost for each model variant. we can create a hypothetical run for the gating policy so you can preview unit economics.
00:07:12 Priya: auditing again — will we get an immutable record of the rollout steps?
00:07:16 Alex: yes, every rollout is logged. we persist the policy, hashes, who triggered it, and timestamps.
00:07:22 Jane: great. one other ask: can Redwood do an initial quick scan (like a heuristic run) to point to likely bad layers?
00:07:28 Samira: yes — we can run a fast 500-sample approximate profiler in about 30-45 minutes that will highlight top 10 suspect layers. that helps prioritize the exhaustive bisect.
00:07:39 Tom: perfect. we'll share the golden outputs now.
00:07:41 Alex: ok recap and next steps — samira does fast profile and then layerwise bisect; diego provisions test node; tom uploads prompts and baseline. we'll share a benchmark schedule and a runbook for KMS + cache encryption. i'll send the precision-gating slide deck.
00:07:58 Priya: one more secops item: if we end up storing per-precision cache shards, can we configure TTL and a purge on-demand?
00:08:06 Diego: yes TTL and purge APIs exist; we'll include retention defaults and an example purge script in the runbook.
00:08:12 Chris: thanks all. any competitors doing this well?
00:08:15 Alex: some vendors expose layer gating but we think our combined runtime+optimize recommendations and the KV-aware fallbacks are differentiated — we'll include a short comparison doc.
00:08:25 Jane: thanks. that's it from our side.
00:08:28 Alex: awesome. we'll follow up with artifacts today. thanks everyone.
